comment: **Six repositories that were released separately, in six languages, pinned by commit.**
A cross-repository question is only a cross-repository question if the repositories are real: a fixture whose
imports the author already knew how to resolve is one repository written twice. These six are downloaded from
GitHub at the commit named here and never committed, so a run measures the revision the file names rather than a
**Pinned by commit and not by tag.** A tag would have been chosen because it looks stable; the commit is what was
in front of the indexer on the day the corpus was built, and the artifact can be re-derived from it exactly.
**The languages are the ones the product claims**, and each brings its own doc-comment convention: Python
docstrings, JSDoc in JavaScript and TypeScript, Javadoc in Java, godoc in Go and rustdoc in Rust. Questions are
derived from those comments, so the corpus tests six conventions rather than six spellings of one.
**Go and Rust are here because the roadmap said they were, and because a language nobody asks a question in is a
language whose claim is untested.** Both were chosen by measurement rather than by reputation: four candidates were
indexed and the two that produced the most documented symbols were kept (`gin` at 407 questions against `cobra` at
**Neither the number of questions a repository yields nor its doc-comment density decides how many it contributes.**
The sample is a quota per repository (`sampleQuestions`), so `ripgrep` - which documents itself roughly three times
as thoroughly as `gson` - is not three times the measurement. A stride over the pool made the previous corpus 67 per
cent `google/gson`, which made every per-repository figure a description of the sample.

repositories.role: typed HTTP client, JSDoc with tags
web framework, godoc on exported identifiers
search tool, rustdoc on public items
